rule: Evidence credits program models, not wording. A code or wording alone never earns more than "possible link, model not confirmed". Only claims an independent verifier fetched, with a verbatim excerpt, enter this file.

tiers.tested: Causal studies of a matching program model.
tiers.research-associated: Consistent correlational evidence (a meta-analysis, or several long-term studies that adjust for earlier achievement or attendance). Worded "is associated with"; earns no credit.
tiers.checked, not supported: The review looked and found no evidence strong enough.

programModels.name: School-day reading tutoring
programModels.description: Tutoring during the school day by paid, trained tutors (teachers or paraprofessionals), at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, with reading as the content. A partner coded Literacy: Reading and Writing (Y1.1) that does not run this model gets no evidence level from this link. Volunteer tutoring counts only at the smaller volunteer-trial size.
programModels.typicalEffect: Pooled gain of 0.29 standard deviations on literacy tests across randomized trials (0.37 for all outcomes in the 2020 working paper); large United States programs (1,000 or more students) about 0.16 standard deviations; volunteer reading tutoring trials 0.10 (Reading Partners) and 0.13 (Experience Corps) standard deviations on reading comprehension. Plan on the at-scale 0.16 standard deviations, not the pooled size.

programModels.name: School-day math tutoring
programModels.description: Tutoring during the school day by paid, trained tutors (teachers or paraprofessionals), at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, with math as the content. A partner coded Mathematics (Y1.3) that does not run this model gets no evidence level from this link.
programModels.typicalEffect: Pooled gain of 0.27 standard deviations on math tests across randomized trials; large United States programs about 0.16 to 0.21 standard deviations.

programModels.name: Daily high school math tutoring with two students per tutor
programModels.description: Daily math tutoring during a school-day class period, two students per paid, trained tutor, for students in grades 9 and 10 (the Saga model, about 40 minutes of tutoring a day).
programModels.typicalEffect: 0.16 standard deviations (first trial, boys only) and 0.37 standard deviations (replication) on math tests for students who took part; 0.18 to 0.40 standard deviations in the journal version. These are effects on participants; the effect of offering the program to all eligible students is smaller and was not retrieved in the checked evidence.

programModels.name: Structured social and emotional learning curriculum taught to whole classes
programModels.description: A named, structured social and emotional learning curriculum (for example Second Step, Positive Action or Caring School Community) taught to whole classes during the school day, sequenced lessons with active practice, for at least a school year. Skill outcomes reported by an enrichment program do not qualify.
programModels.typicalEffect: About 0.10 standard deviations across test scores and grades combined (2025 meta-analysis, grades 1-12); 11 percentile points on academic performance (2011 meta-analysis). The evidence is for teacher-delivered classroom curricula, not for skill gains that partners report.

programModels.name: Brief belonging writing exercise at the start of middle school
programModels.description: Two brief, scripted classroom writing exercises at the start of middle school that frame worries about belonging as normal and temporary, delivered to whole sixth-grade classes. We expect this to be rare among partners.
programModels.typicalEffect: 12 percent fewer absences than the control group, plus 18 percent fewer D and F grades and 34 percent fewer behavior referrals; cost about 1.35 dollars per student.

programModels.name: Personalized messages to families about their own child's absences
programModels.description: Repeated, personalized mailings, postcards or texts to a family about their own child's absences, drawn from school records under a data-sharing agreement. General family events and engagement policies do not qualify.
programModels.typicalEffect: Chronic absence down 10 to 15 percent; total absences down 2.4 percent (single postcard, Philadelphia), 6 percent (best mailing, Philadelphia) and 1.9 percent across six district-run trials; class attendance up 12 percent with weekly texts.

programModels.name: Lead agency of a whole-school community school
programModels.description: The partner is the lead agency or full-time coordinator of a whole-school community school, with on-site health, family and learning services, sustained for at least three years. Credit belongs at the organization level, not to individual outcome statements.
programModels.typicalEffect: Chronic absence down 7.4 percentage points (elementary and middle) and 8.3 points (high school), three-year average.

programModels.name: Paid summer job placement for high school students
programModels.description: A paid summer job placement (wages paid, several weeks) for low-income high school students, ideally allocated or evaluated by lottery.
programModels.typicalEffect: On-time graduation up 4.4 percentage points and dropout down 2.5 points over four years among Boston lottery applicants (journal; working paper 6.1 and 2.6).

programModels.name: Ninth grade on-track monitoring from school records
programModels.description: A program serving ninth graders that tracks its own students' course passing and credits from school records (for example through a data-sharing agreement) and acts on them.
programModels.typicalEffect: Philadelphia: 82 percent graduation on track against 56 percent off track (87.8 to 89.2 against 43.3 to 48.8 percent in district cohorts); Chicago: on-track students 3.5 times more likely to graduate.

pathways.summary: Tutoring programs that build children's reading skills raise scores on standardized reading tests, the skill the state English language arts test measures.
pathways.programModel: Tutoring during the school day by paid, trained tutors (teachers or paraprofessionals), at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, with reading as the content. A partner coded Literacy: Reading and Writing (Y1.1) that does not run this model gets no evidence level from this link. Volunteer tutoring counts only at the smaller volunteer-trial size.
pathways.typicalEffect: Pooled gain of 0.29 standard deviations on literacy tests across randomized trials (0.37 for all outcomes in the 2020 working paper); large United States programs (1,000 or more students) about 0.16 standard deviations; volunteer reading tutoring trials 0.10 (Reading Partners) and 0.13 (Experience Corps) standard deviations on reading comprehension. Plan on the at-scale 0.16 standard deviations, not the pooled size.
pathways.caveats: Outcomes were study-administered or national standardized reading tests, not the Pennsylvania test. At scale, effects are a third to a half of the full-sample size. Effects were larger for teacher and paraprofessional tutors, earlier grades and school-day delivery, and smaller after school. The scale meta-analysis covers kindergarten to grade 12 in wealthy (OECD) countries, not only the United States. Volunteer programs often assign two or more tutors per child by design. Bounded by the after-school reading null and negative results (structured after-school reading row) and the 21st Century Community Learning Centers null.

pathways.summary: Tutoring programs that build children's math skills raise scores on standardized math tests, the skill the state math test measures.
pathways.programModel: Tutoring during the school day by paid, trained tutors (teachers or paraprofessionals), at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, with math as the content. A partner coded Mathematics (Y1.3) that does not run this model gets no evidence level from this link.
pathways.typicalEffect: Pooled gain of 0.27 standard deviations on math tests across randomized trials; large United States programs about 0.16 to 0.21 standard deviations.
pathways.caveats: Outcomes were not the Pennsylvania test. At scale, effects are a third to a half of the full-sample size. Smaller for after-school and nonprofessional tutors. Bounded by the structured after-school math result that faded (its own row) and the 21st Century Community Learning Centers null.

pathways.summary: Daily small-group math tutoring in ninth and tenth grade raises high school math test scores, the skill the Algebra I end-of-course exam measures.
pathways.programModel: Daily math tutoring during a school-day class period, two students per paid, trained tutor, for students in grades 9 and 10 (the Saga model, about 40 minutes of tutoring a day).
pathways.typicalEffect: 0.16 standard deviations (first trial, boys only) and 0.37 standard deviations (replication) on math tests for students who took part; 0.18 to 0.40 standard deviations in the journal version. These are effects on participants; the effect of offering the program to all eligible students is smaller and was not retrieved in the checked evidence.
pathways.caveats: One program (Saga) in Chicago; the first trial enrolled boys only. The test was not the Keystone Algebra I exam. Tutoring was about 40 minutes a day, not a full hour. The general tutoring meta-analysis supports math gains but found larger effects in earlier grades.

pathways.summary: Daily math tutoring cuts math course failures, and passing ninth-grade courses strongly predicts graduating in four years in Philadelphia and Chicago.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: not used for credit. Tested model: the Saga daily school-day tutoring model (see L-03).
pathways.typicalEffect: On-time graduation +1.9 percentage points for participants (standard error 3.4) against a 77.2 percent control mean, not significant; the range runs from a 4.8-point decline to an 8.6-point gain.
pathways.caveats: Correction: the draft said graduation was not measured. The same paper estimated on-time graduation directly: +1.9 points (standard error 3.4), not significant (Guryan and others 2021, working paper 21-12, pages 6 and 22, fetched by the methods reviewer at https://www.ipr.northwestern.edu/documents/working-papers/2021/wp-21-12.pdf). Non-math failures fell only in the first trial. The attendance gain in the researcher's note was contradicted by the checker.

pathways.summary: Daily math tutoring did not change how many days students were absent.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No significant effect on days absent (first trial: plus 1.58 days, standard error 1.87).
pathways.caveats: The researcher's claim of attendance gains was contradicted by the paper itself.

pathways.summary: Classroom-based summer reading programs for low-income children modestly raise reading comprehension.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: classroom summer reading instruction for low-income children, focused on comprehension.
pathways.typicalEffect: Overall gain of 0.10 standard deviations on total reading; 0.20 on reading comprehension for mostly low-income samples; about zero for mixed-income samples.
pathways.caveats: The checker did not confirm that all included studies were randomized. Gains were limited to low-income samples. The national summer learning trial's randomized effect faded (its own row). Bounded by L-07: the national summer learning trial's randomized effect was gone by the spring state test.

pathways.summary: Voluntary summer learning programs gave a small, short-lived math gain; state test advantages appeared only among students who attended often, which is a correlational finding.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Randomized offer: 0.08 standard deviations in math on a fall study test, gone by spring; students attending 20 or more days: 0.14 math and 0.09 English language arts on state tests after a second summer, not significant by grade 7.
pathways.caveats: Dosage thresholds were 25 hours of math or 34 hours of English language arts a year. The attender comparison is not randomized. Effects faded.

pathways.summary: Out-of-school-time programs with real academic instruction raise reading and math achievement a little, most when certified teachers teach or tutoring is included.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: academic instruction in reading or math led by certified teachers, or including reading tutoring, for low-achieving students.
pathways.typicalEffect: Small but significant reading and math gains (out-of-school-time meta-analysis; sizes not in the abstract); increased learning time with certified teachers: literacy 0.18 and math 0.09 standard deviations; with traditional instruction: literacy 0.14 and math 0.10.
pathways.caveats: Both meta-analyses mix randomized and comparison-group studies. The certified-teacher and traditional-instruction conditions were tested one at a time, not together. All effects were below 0.25 standard deviations. The researcher's note of harm for students with behavior problems was not confirmed. Bounded by the 21st Century Community Learning Centers null and the structured after-school reading result.

pathways.summary: A structured after-school math curriculum raised math scores slightly for one year, but not in the second cohort or after a second year.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: 0.09 standard deviations after one year in the first cohort; not significant in the second cohort; no added benefit from a second year.
pathways.caveats: Results come from 15 math centers only. The 48 hours is the extra instruction over the control group.

pathways.summary: Structured after-school reading instruction did not raise reading scores, and a two-year offer lowered them.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No effect after one year; minus 0.17 standard deviations on total reading after a two-year offer; Higher Achievement reading comprehension 0.04 standard deviations, not significant.
pathways.caveats: The comparison group received homework help and other services. This row bounds the reading tutoring and out-of-school-time academic rows.

pathways.summary: An intensive multi-year after-school and summer academic program raised math problem-solving scores four years later.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: the Higher Achievement model: intensive multi-year after-school and summer academic program starting in grade 5 or 6.
pathways.typicalEffect: 0.11 standard deviations on math problem solving in year 4.
pathways.caveats: Reading did not improve in the same trial. The test was a national standardized test. Washington, DC and Alexandria, Virginia. The researcher's 'later expansion study' was not confirmed.

pathways.summary: General after-school centers with little academic time did not change test scores, grades or homework completion.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No impact on test scores, grades or homework completion in either of two years.
pathways.caveats: Program design dates from before 2002. Bounds every after-school academic row.

pathways.summary: Universal social and emotional learning curricula taught during the school day raise students' test scores and grades slightly.
pathways.programModel: A named, structured social and emotional learning curriculum (for example Second Step, Positive Action or Caring School Community) taught to whole classes during the school day, sequenced lessons with active practice, for at least a school year. Skill outcomes reported by an enrichment program do not qualify.
pathways.typicalEffect: About 0.10 standard deviations across test scores and grades combined (2025 meta-analysis, grades 1-12); 11 percentile points on academic performance (2011 meta-analysis). The evidence is for teacher-delivered classroom curricula, not for skill gains that partners report.
pathways.caveats: The share of randomized studies was not confirmed. Achievement mixes grades and tests, and no study used the state tests or the Keystone exams. Pooled effects are likely inflated by publication bias. Communication (Y4.6) and Teamwork (Y4.7) are left out because no study tested them against an indicator. The domain-only code Y4 was removed on the methods reviewer's advice.

pathways.summary: Social and emotional learning gains persist years later, but graduation was rarely measured.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Academic performance about 13 percentile points higher at follow-up (mean about 3.5 years later); no graduation estimate.
pathways.caveats: Graduation is 'infrequently assessed'. Facts were checked against a summary by one author's organization.

pathways.summary: Cognitive behavioral group sessions that teach adolescent boys to slow down automatic reactions raised graduation in the first trial.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: the Becoming a Man cognitive behavioral group curriculum for adolescent boys, with trained counselors, in school.
pathways.typicalEffect: Graduation up 6 to 9 percentage points (12 to 19 percent), first trial only; arrests down 28 to 35 percent during the program.
pathways.caveats: Graduation was measured in the first trial only. The two later trials found no significant effect on student outcomes (own row); across four trials school engagement rose 0.03 to 0.08 standard deviations. Boys only, Chicago. Dropout counts were not measured separately. Researchers also mapped this program to mental health, violence and justice codes (Y8.6, Y8.12, Y8.13). Merged reading: one trial raised graduation; two later trials at new sites found no effect on student outcomes (L-16).

pathways.summary: The same cognitive behavioral program at new sites showed no significant effect on student outcomes.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No statistically significant effect on student outcomes in the two later trials.
pathways.caveats: Program summary page, not a paper. Bounds the Becoming a Man graduation row.

pathways.summary: Brief classroom exercises that frame worries about belonging as normal at the start of middle school cut absences.
pathways.programModel: Two brief, scripted classroom writing exercises at the start of middle school that frame worries about belonging as normal and temporary, delivered to whole sixth-grade classes. We expect this to be rare among partners.
pathways.typicalEffect: 12 percent fewer absences than the control group, plus 18 percent fewer D and F grades and 34 percent fewer behavior referrals; cost about 1.35 dollars per student.
pathways.caveats: One district-wide trial (11 middle schools in a Midwestern district). The absence figure is a relative change, not attendance-rate points.

pathways.summary: A belonging exercise cut discipline citations for Black boys through high school, and early misbehavior is one of the flags that predict not graduating in Philadelphia.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Discipline citations down 65 percent among Black boys (confidence interval 15 to 85 percent); no graduation estimate.
pathways.caveats: Only the second experiment (137 sixth graders) tested the belonging exercise alone. Discipline is not a SPOTlight indicator. The behavior flag is not a well-replicated stand-alone predictor in the checked sources.

pathways.summary: High schools that raise students' social well-being and effort raise graduation, beyond their effects on test scores.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Per standard deviation of school effect: graduation up about 1.5 percentage points (social well-being) and 1.6 (effort).
pathways.caveats: School value-added models (observational), not programs. Chicago ninth graders. Self-reported measures.

pathways.summary: Teachers who improve students' attendance, behavior and grades raise later outcomes such as finishing high school, beyond their test-score effects.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Adding non-test measures more than doubles the predictable variation in teacher effects on longer-run outcomes.
pathways.caveats: Teacher effects in North Carolina ninth grade, not a program.

pathways.summary: Writing about personal values, meant to ease stereotype threat, did not raise academic performance in a large replication.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No detectable effect; the estimates rule out benefits larger than 0.10 standard deviations.
pathways.caveats: Outcome was grades and related measures, not state tests.

pathways.summary: Mentoring gives small gains across many kinds of outcomes, but academic gains from school-based mentoring faded by the second year.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: About 9 percentile points across all outcomes combined (2011 meta-analysis); a modest overall effect (2019 meta-analysis); school-based mentoring academic gain after year 1, not sustained into year 2.
pathways.caveats: No academic-specific or test-score effect was retrieved from the meta-analyses. Larger effects for youth with existing difficulties.

pathways.summary: A trained monitor who tracks each student's attendance, behavior and grades and steps in early keeps students in school.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: Check and Connect: a trained monitor checks attendance, behavior and grades and intervenes, from ninth grade, tested with students with learning, emotional or behavioral disabilities.
pathways.typicalEffect: Staying in school up 25 percentile points (range 18 to 31) on the What Works Clearinghouse improvement index.
pathways.caveats: Two small randomized trials (238 Minneapolis students); the Clearinghouse rates the extent of evidence as small. No effect on completing school (own row). Bounded by L-24: no discernible effect on completing school.

pathways.summary: The same monitoring and mentoring program showed no discernible effect on completing school.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Completing school: no discernible effect (improvement index plus 1, one study).
pathways.caveats: One underpowered study. Bounds the Check and Connect dropout row.

pathways.summary: Trained mentors who check in with chronically absent students added school days and kept more high school students enrolled.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: About 9 more days a year per previously chronically absent mentored student; mentored high school students 52 percent more likely to remain in school the next year.
pathways.caveats: Comparison of 100 pilot schools with 46 comparison schools; selection into mentoring is not addressed. New York City. Promising; would move up with a randomized or stronger comparison design.

pathways.summary: Warm teacher-student relationships go with more engagement, which partly carries a small link to achievement.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Medium to large associations with engagement and small to medium with achievement (no correlation values in the fetched abstract).
pathways.caveats: Correlational; teachers, not program staff.

pathways.summary: Students attending more school days is exactly what this indicator counts. This is a definition, not evidence that any program type moves attendance.
pathways.programModel: Any program, provided the partner shows from school records that its participants' share at or above 90 percent of days rose against a comparison group. A program model with a tested attendance effect (L-28, L-36) gives a reason to expect it; other models need their own data.
pathways.typicalEffect: Not applicable: the size depends on the program. Program models with tested attendance effects are in L-28 (messages to families) and L-36 (community schools).
pathways.caveats: The trial figures in the draft belong to L-28 and were removed here. Chronic absence (missing 10 percent or more of days) is close to the complement of this indicator, but District enrollment rules can differ. School asthma education (L-66), school health centers (L-65) and tutoring (L-05) did not move school-record attendance, so a program type alone is no reason to expect a gain.

pathways.summary: Personalized messages to parents about their own child's absences correct parents' underestimates, and their children then miss fewer days.
pathways.programModel: Repeated, personalized mailings, postcards or texts to a family about their own child's absences, drawn from school records under a data-sharing agreement. General family events and engagement policies do not qualify.
pathways.typicalEffect: Chronic absence down 10 to 15 percent; total absences down 2.4 percent (single postcard, Philadelphia), 6 percent (best mailing, Philadelphia) and 1.9 percent across six district-run trials; class attendance up 12 percent with weekly texts.
pathways.caveats: Messages came from districts, not partners. Family Connection and Trust with the Program (F1.8) was removed: trust was not tested. The postcard trial's window was 43 school days. The comparison with earlier effect sizes in the six-trial study could not be checked.

pathways.summary: Frequent messages to parents about missed work, grades and absences kept more students enrolled.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: weekly teacher-to-parent messages or automated texts about missed assignments, grades and absences.
pathways.typicalEffect: Share failing to earn course credit fell from 15.8 to 9.3 percent, mainly by preventing dropout (summer credit recovery); retention rose with weekly texts.
pathways.caveats: Short-run staying enrolled, not the annual dropout count. One trial was a summer credit-recovery program; the other was in Kanawha County, West Virginia.

pathways.summary: Frequent messages to parents cut course failures, and passing ninth-grade courses predicts four-year graduation in Philadelphia.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: weekly teacher-to-parent messages or automated texts about missed assignments, grades and absences.
pathways.typicalEffect: Course failures down 27 percent; on-track Philadelphia ninth graders graduated at 82 percent against 56 percent off track.
pathways.caveats: Graduation was not measured in the trials. Staying enrolled is not the same as graduating.

pathways.summary: Information to parents about their child's schoolwork raised math scores in one high school trial but did not move state test scores in a larger trial.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: West Virginia: no impact on state tests. Los Angeles high school students: math up 0.21 standard deviations, English up 0.04 (not significant), grade point average up 0.19 standard deviations.
pathways.caveats: The positive trial was one school, high school only. Messages moved attendance and course passing more than proficiency.

pathways.summary: Relationship-building home visits go with less chronic absence in one multi-district study, but not in another district's evaluation.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: 21 percent lower odds of chronic absence for visited students; schools visiting 10 percent or more of families had 35 percent higher odds of English language arts proficiency; Washoe County found no relationship.
pathways.caveats: Correlational; families may be chosen for visits because of poor attendance. The proficiency link is for school-level implementation, not individual visits.

pathways.summary: A multifamily group program in Philadelphia kindergartens did not change parents' social support or children's academic learning.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No significant effects on any key outcome in the randomized trial, including parental social support and academic learning.
pathways.caveats: Among families attending 3 or more sessions (non-randomized), reading was higher at the end of grade 1 but kindergarten attendance was lower. The social-capital gain in the researcher's note came from a different trial in San Antonio and Phoenix.

pathways.summary: Parental involvement, especially high expectations, goes with higher achievement, and parental involvement programs go with gains.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: About 0.5 to 0.55 standard deviations across academic measures (2007 meta-analysis, urban secondary students); about 0.3 standard deviations for programs (2012).
pathways.caveats: The studies are largely associations; the randomized share was not established. Bounded by the Philadelphia family-program null.

pathways.summary: Mothers' education raised young children's school readiness, but no checked study links readiness to the grade 3 state test.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Eight months of maternal education: school readiness up 0.21 standard deviations.
pathways.caveats: The treatment was any education activity, not adult basic education alone. Only one corpus statement.

pathways.summary: Community schools that coordinate health, family and learning services on site cut chronic absence.
pathways.programModel: The partner is the lead agency or full-time coordinator of a whole-school community school, with on-site health, family and learning services, sustained for at least three years. Credit belongs at the organization level, not to individual outcome statements.
pathways.typicalEffect: Chronic absence down 7.4 percentage points (elementary and middle) and 8.3 points (high school), three-year average.
pathways.caveats: Matched comparison schools, not randomized; New York City model (its funding level was not in the checked evidence). All community schools had positive effects, with Renewal schools strongest. Philadelphia's own initiative has no impact estimate: its year 1 evaluation found broad outcomes without measures.

pathways.summary: Community schools raised credit accumulation and graduation compared with similar schools.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: a whole-school community school sustained for three years (see L-36).
pathways.typicalEffect: Graduation 4.9 percentage points higher than comparison schools over three years (7.2 in year 3); credit accumulation up in all three years.
pathways.caveats: The graduation figure comes from the New York City schools' own summary of the RAND study. Credit accumulation, which RAND did confirm, is a neighbor of graduation, not the indicator.

pathways.summary: Community schools raised math scores by the third year.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: a whole-school community school sustained for three years (see L-36).
pathways.typicalEffect: Average 0.066 standard deviations on state math tests (significant); 0.131 in year 3; years 1 and 2 not significant.
pathways.caveats: Only year 3 was significant on its own.

pathways.summary: Community schools did not significantly raise English language arts scores over three years.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Positive but not significant in all three years.
pathways.caveats: RAND reports non-significant positive estimates, not evidence of no effect.

pathways.summary: Elementary-school coordinators who link each child to tailored supports went with lower later high school dropout.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Dropout 9.2 percent against 16.6 percent (about half the odds).
pathways.caveats: Propensity-weighted comparison, developer-run, in Boston; City Connects students began with lower report-card scores. Middle school test gains come from program pages only; the grade point average claim was not confirmed. Promising; needs independent replication.

pathways.summary: Case management and early-warning school reform improved attitudes or the share of students with no warning flags, but not attendance, course passing or graduation.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Communities In Schools trial: no improvement in attendance, achievement or behavior; Diplomas Now trial: more students with no early-warning flag (mostly sixth grade), no effect on average attendance or for ninth graders.
pathways.caveats: Communities In Schools whole-school graduation rose equally in comparison schools. A review of integrated student supports found a mix of positive and null results and almost no negative ones.

pathways.summary: Collective-impact networks have no measured causal effect on student outcomes.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No effect sizes; communities with the most infrastructure growth tended to see more indicators improve.
pathways.caveats: Commissioned evaluation; authors say the results are not definitive.

pathways.summary: After-school programs that use sequenced, active, focused and explicit practices show test-score gains that other programs do not.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: 0.20 standard deviations on achievement tests for programs using the practices against 0.02 for others.
pathways.caveats: The quality comparison is between studies, not tested within a study. Program quality appears as a condition on the social and emotional learning row instead.

pathways.summary: Middle schoolers who took part in a citywide after-school system had fewer school absences two years later.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: About 25 percent fewer absences after two years.
pathways.caveats: Propensity-matched comparison in Providence. A2.5 is a program output (participation), not an outcome. Other benefits faded by year 2.

pathways.summary: Coaching that changes how adults teach raises students' achievement.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: sustained observation-and-feedback coaching of classroom teachers of reading or math.
pathways.typicalEffect: 0.18 standard deviations on student achievement; larger programs show only a fraction of that.
pathways.caveats: Tested with classroom teachers (mostly literacy coaching in pre-kindergarten and elementary), not out-of-school-time staff. The 0.20 figure for content-specific coaching was not verified.

pathways.summary: Tutoring by teachers and paraprofessionals produces larger gains than tutoring by volunteers or parents, which suggests that tutor skill matters.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Effects largest for teacher and paraprofessional tutors (pooled 0.29 standard deviations overall).

For self-efficacy, a meta-analysis found that in children only earlier performance predicts later self-efficacy, not the reverse. A 2024 reanalysis argues that adjusting for an earlier score can produce spurious effects of this kind.

pathways.summary: Failing courses and low grades in the middle grades or ninth grade are associated with later dropping out, beyond what eighth-grade test scores and background predict.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: In Philadelphia, sixth graders who failed math were 54 percent less likely to graduate, and those who failed English 42 percent less likely. In Chicago, freshman grades and course failures explained about 39 percent of the variation in graduation, against about 12 percent for test scores and background.
pathways.caveats: These are early-warning predictions, not effects of raising grades. Most studies count students who did not graduate rather than the District's dropout count. The Philadelphia cohorts are from the 1990s and 2000s.

pathways.summary: Low attendance in the middle grades or ninth grade is associated with later dropping out, alongside course failure and test scores.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Philadelphia sixth graders attending 80 percent of days or less were 68 percent less likely to graduate. In a large secondary-school study, 10 ninth-grade absences went with about a 1 percentage point lower on-time graduation rate, after adjusting for earlier test scores and grades.
pathways.caveats: Early-warning predictions, not effects of a program. The Philadelphia model controls for the other warning flags but not earlier test scores. Most studies count students who did not graduate rather than the District's dropout count. Attendance itself is already the attendance indicator, so this adds the later dropout association only.

pathways.summary: More absences are associated with lower grade 3 reading and math scores, even comparing each student with their own record over time.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: In North Carolina, each absence lowered grade 3 math by about 0.0025 and reading by about 0.0015 of a standard deviation, about three times more by grade 5. Ten fewer absences across grades went with about 5.5 percent of a standard deviation higher math and 2.9 percent higher reading.
pathways.caveats: Effects per absence are small; they add up for chronically absent students. In Philadelphia the harm was mainly from unexcused absences and mainly in math. Attendance itself is the attendance indicator; this adds the test-score association.

pathways.summary: Students graduating within four years of first entering ninth grade is exactly what this indicator counts. This is a definition, not evidence that any program type raises graduation.
pathways.programModel: Any program, provided the partner shows from school records that its own students graduated within four years at a higher rate than a comparison group. A program model with a tested graduation effect (paid summer jobs) gives a reason to expect it; other models need their own data.
pathways.typicalEffect: Not applicable: the size depends on the program. The program model with a tested graduation effect is paid summer jobs for high school students; attendance gains may also help a little.
pathways.caveats: Added 2026-10-18 after the review, on a lead from the extractor export thread: the attendance identity had a row and the graduation identity did not. The basis is the SPOTlight wording in Severin's 2026-10-18 paste, not a study. Reaching dropouts was not added: whether a student who re-enrolls leaves the District dropout count depends on District enrollment rules that were not checked. Monitoring and mentoring (Check and Connect) and case management did not raise completion in the checked trials.

pathways.summary: Attention, task persistence and impulse control at school entry are associated with higher later reading and math scores, beyond children's early academic skills.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Effects are small. Early math skills predicted later scores most, then reading, then attention. In a national study, kindergarten executive functions predicted grade 2 scores by about 0.05 to 0.12 of a standard deviation after earlier achievement.
pathways.caveats: Holds for young children only: in two middle-school studies, self-control did not predict changes in test scores once earlier scores were counted (it did predict report-card grades). Academic Perseverance (Y1.10) fits early task persistence; Emotion Regulation and Coping (Y4.2) fits only its impulse-control part. Social skills and prosocial behavior were not associated with later scores in the same studies.

pathways.summary: High schools where students report better relationships with teachers are associated with fewer students dropping out, after accounting for tenth-grade math scores and background.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: In one study, a school one standard deviation higher on student-teacher relations had about 86 percent lower odds of a student dropping out, but only in schools under 1,500 students. In the other, a better relationship climate went with lower dropout by senior year.
pathways.caveats: This is about a whole school's relationship climate, not one student's mentor or relationship. In the first study the association disappeared in schools over 1,500 students, which matters for large Philadelphia high schools. Both studies count dropping out by senior year, not the four-year graduation rate. A meta-analysis of unadjusted associations found only a non-significant trend for poor teacher relationships and dropout. The same studies found no association with test-score gains.

pathways.summary: Students who do their homework, take part and pay attention in class are associated with lower dropout, compared with students at the same achievement level.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: In the national sample, teacher-rated academic engagement (standardized coefficient about -0.27) and student-reported behavioral engagement (about -0.30) each predicted lower dropout by grade 12, with test achievement (about -0.20) in the same model.
pathways.caveats: Narrow: two studies. In the national sample, achievement was measured at the same time as engagement, not before it, and behavioral engagement includes skipping and lateness, which overlaps attendance.

Paper presented at the Harvard Civil Rights Project conference, January 13, 2001 (ERIC ED458694). Published version: American Educational Research Journal, 40(2), 353-393 (2003), doi:10.3102/00028312040002353.

A-001.population_location: 3,840 students in 190 public, Catholic and independent high schools in the 30 largest US metropolitan areas
